about: The scripted AI lesson for g5-uk-economy (2026-11-19, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions on the sectors, from g5-nigeria.

keyPoints.heading: Causes of economic change in the UK

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about how the UK's economy has changed, what the new economy looks like, and how the change affects the environment, the countryside and different regions.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. An economy has sectors: primary takes raw materials, secondary makes things, tertiary provides services. Which sector is a car factory in?

wrong.primary: Not quite: primary takes raw materials from the land or sea. A factory makes things: secondary.
wrong.tertiary: Not quite: tertiary provides services. A factory makes things: secondary.

idk.hint: Does a car factory take raw materials, make things, or provide a service?

steps.answerWhy: A car factory makes things, so it is in the secondary sector.

steps.question: Second: a nurse works in which sector?
steps.right: Yes: a nurse provides a service, so tertiary.

wrong.primary: Not quite: a nurse does not take raw materials. Health care is a service: tertiary.
wrong.secondary: Not quite: a nurse does not make things. Health care is a service: tertiary.

idk.hint: Tertiary is the sector that provides services. Is caring for patients a service?

steps.answerWhy: A nurse provides a service, so works in the tertiary sector.

steps.text: Now this lesson. In the past, many people in Britain worked in coal mines, steelworks, shipyards and textile mills: heavy, dirty work. These old industries are called traditional industries.

The decline of these industries and of factory work, and the loss of their jobs, is called deindustrialisation. Coal and iron ore, the rock iron is made from, ran out or became costly to dig, and machines replaced many workers.
The way countries have become more connected through trade, travel and communication is called globalisation.

steps.question: Predict: with globalisation, goods made abroad could easily be shipped to the UK. What would that do to many UK factories?

options.text: Many closed, because goods were made more cheaply abroad

steps.right: Yes: factories abroad paid lower wages, so they could make goods more cheaply, and many UK factories closed.

wrong.other: Not quite: many closed, because goods were made more cheaply abroad.
wrong.grew: Not quite: they faced cheaper goods from abroad, so many closed.
wrong.same: Not quite: cheaper goods from abroad meant many UK factories closed.

idk.hint: If the same goods could be made more cheaply abroad, who would buyers choose?

steps.answerWhy: Goods were made more cheaply where wages were lower, so many UK factories closed.

steps.text: The government's choices, its policies, mattered too. Governments stopped paying to keep open industries that cost more to run than they earned, such as coal mines, and encouraged service industries such as banking instead.
Three causes, then, changed the UK's economy: deindustrialisation, globalisation and government policies.
Whole towns built around a mine or a steelworks lost their main employer. Some, in places such as South Yorkshire and South Wales, still have high unemployment.

steps.prompt: In one line: give the three causes of economic change in the UK.
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the UK's economy changed because of deindustrialisation, globalisation and government policies.

steps.text: An economy where most people work in services, not factories, mines or farms, is called a post-industrial economy. The UK is one.
In 2025 services made up about 73% of the UK's economy, manufacturing about 8%, and farming, forestry and fishing under 1%.
The UK's GNI per head, its mean income per person, was $54,550 a year in 2025.
The growing parts are information technology, finance (banking and insurance, especially in London), other services such as retail (shops) and health, and research.
Work based on knowledge and research is called the quaternary sector: a fourth sector, after primary, secondary and tertiary.

steps.question: Which job is in the quaternary sector?

options.text: A worker in a car factory

steps.right: Yes: research is knowledge work, the quaternary sector.

wrong.other: Not quite: a scientist researching new medicines.
wrong.factory: Not quite: a car factory makes things, the secondary sector. Research is quaternary.
wrong.farmer: Not quite: farming is primary. Research is quaternary.

idk.hint: The quaternary sector is about knowledge and research. Which job is research?

steps.answerWhy: Researching new medicines is knowledge work, in the quaternary sector.

steps.text: A group of research and high-tech companies built together, usually next to a university, is called a science park.
Firms in a science park can share ideas with the university and hire its graduates, students who have finished their degrees. They also want main roads nearby, space to grow and green surroundings.
Cambridge Science Park, beside the University of Cambridge and close to main roads, is home to many technology and medical research companies.
A group of offices and small, clean workshops on the edge of a town, near main roads, is called a business park.

steps.question: Which site would suit a new science park best?

options.text: Next to a university, beside a motorway junction
In a remote valley far from any road
In a crowded old town centre with no space

steps.right: Yes: the university gives ideas and graduates, and the motorway makes it easy to reach.

wrong.other: Not quite: next to a university, beside a motorway junction.
wrong.remote: Not quite: staff and visitors need to reach it. A site by a university and a motorway is best.
wrong.nospace: Not quite: science parks need space to grow. A site by a university and a motorway is best.

idk.hint: Science parks want a university, good roads and space. Which site has them?

steps.answerWhy: A site next to a university and a motorway junction gives ideas, graduates and easy access.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the UK's post-industrial economy based on?
points: knowledge and research work (the quaternary sector)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the UK's post-industrial economy is mostly services, with growing knowledge and research work in places such as science parks.

steps.text: Industry can harm the physical environment. Old mines and steelworks left scarred land, waste heaps and polluted rivers. Factories still use energy, make waste and give off pollution.
Industry that does as little harm as possible to the environment, so it stays healthy for the future, is called environmentally sustainable.
Burning coal, oil or gas, called fossil fuels, for power gives off carbon dioxide, a gas that warms the climate.
Energy from sources that do not run out, such as the Sun and the wind, is called renewable energy. Making electricity from the Sun or wind gives off no carbon dioxide.
Toyota's car factory at Burnaston, near Derby, is one example of more sustainable industry. It aims to run on solar and wind power and to cut its waste.
Part of the Burnaston site has been made into a wildlife reserve, together with the Derbyshire Wildlife Trust.

steps.question: Why does running on solar and wind power make the Burnaston factory more sustainable?

options.text: It burns less fossil fuel, so it gives off less carbon dioxide
It lets the factory make more cars

steps.right: Yes: less fossil fuel burned means less carbon dioxide.

wrong.other: Not quite: it burns less fossil fuel, so it gives off less carbon dioxide.
wrong.more: Not quite: the number of cars is not the point. Solar and wind mean less fossil fuel burned, so less carbon dioxide.
wrong.free: Not quite: solar panels and wind turbines cost money. The gain is less fossil fuel burned, so less carbon dioxide.

idk.hint: Solar and wind replace burning fuel. Does that mean more or less carbon dioxide?

steps.answerWhy: Solar and wind power replace burning fossil fuels, so the factory gives off less carbon dioxide.

steps.text: No factory is completely green. Building it, and bringing in materials and workers, still uses energy and causes pollution.

steps.prompt: In one line: give one way modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable, and say how it helps.
points: a way, such as renewable energy, less waste or a wildlife reserve
how it helps, such as less carbon dioxide or more wildlife
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: a factory such as Toyota at Burnaston can use solar and wind power, which means less carbon dioxide from burning fuel.

steps.text: Rural means in the countryside. The rural landscape is changing in two different ways.
In an area of population growth, such as South Cambridgeshire, near Cambridge, people move in because jobs and good transport are close.

In South Cambridgeshire new housing estates are built and house prices rise, so some local young people cannot afford to buy. Traffic gets busier, but village shops and schools gain customers and pupils.
People, especially the young, leaving the countryside for towns and cities is called rural depopulation. It happens in the Outer Hebrides, islands off north-west Scotland.
In the Outer Hebrides, young people leave to find work and study, so the population that stays is older. Shops, schools and bus services close because too few people use them.

steps.question: A village has a growing number of empty homes, and its bus service has just been cut. Which kind of area is it more likely to be?

options.text: An area of population decline, like the Outer Hebrides
An area of population growth, like South Cambridgeshire

steps.right: Yes: empty homes and fewer services are signs of people leaving.

wrong.other: Not quite: an area of population decline, like the Outer Hebrides.
wrong.growth: Not quite: in growing areas homes fill up and services gain users. Empty homes and a cut bus point to decline, like the Outer Hebrides.
wrong.city: Not quite: the question is about a village, a rural area. Empty homes and a cut bus point to decline, like the Outer Hebrides.

idk.hint: Are empty homes and fewer buses signs of people arriving or leaving?

steps.answerWhy: Empty homes and cut services are signs of rural depopulation, as in the Outer Hebrides.

steps.text: Tourism and wind farms bring some new jobs to the Outer Hebrides.

steps.prompt: In one line: give one change where the rural population is growing and one where it is falling.
points: where it is growing, such as rising house prices or new estates
where it is falling, such as schools, shops or buses closing
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in growing South Cambridgeshire house prices rise, while in the shrinking Outer Hebrides schools close as young people leave.

steps.text: The basic networks a country needs to work, such as roads, railways, ports and airports, are called infrastructure.
Better infrastructure can help the economy: firms can move goods and people more easily, and building new projects creates jobs.
Busy motorways and main roads are widened. HS2, a high-speed railway, is being built from London to Birmingham; its planned northern sections were cancelled.

Liverpool2 is a new deep-water dock at the Port of Liverpool for the biggest container ships, which carry goods in large metal boxes. Bigger ships carry more goods each trip, which makes trade cheaper.
Heathrow airport has plans for a third runway. Supporters say it would bring more flights and trade; opponents worry about noise, pollution and cost.

steps.question: Why could Liverpool2 help the economy of north-west England?

options.text: Bigger ships can bring and take goods, so firms nearby can trade more cheaply
It will mainly be used by holiday cruises
It moves jobs from Liverpool to London

steps.right: Yes: cheaper, easier trade attracts firms and jobs to the area.

wrong.other: Not quite: bigger ships mean cheaper trade for firms nearby.
wrong.cruise: Not quite: it is built for container ships carrying goods. Cheaper trade attracts firms and jobs.
wrong.london: Not quite: it brings trade to Liverpool. Cheaper trade attracts firms and jobs to the north-west.

idk.hint: Container ships carry goods. What does letting the biggest ones in do for firms nearby?

steps.answerWhy: Bigger ships make trade cheaper for firms nearby, attracting businesses and jobs.

steps.text: The gap in wealth and health between the generally richer south-east of England and much of the rest of the UK is called the north–south divide. On average, people in London and the South East earn more and live longer.
Much of the post-industrial growth came to the south, while many northern towns lost their traditional industries.
Handing powers and money from the national government to a region or city, such as an elected mayor in Greater Manchester, is called devolution. It is one strategy to close the divide.
An area where the government gives businesses lower taxes and simpler rules, to encourage them to set up there, is called an enterprise zone.
Better transport between northern cities is another strategy to close the divide.

steps.question: The government wants a car parts firm to open in a poor northern town. Which strategy would help most?

options.text: Making the town an enterprise zone
Raising business taxes in the north

steps.right: Yes: lower taxes there make the town more attractive to the firm.

wrong.other: Not quite: making the town an enterprise zone.
wrong.london: Not quite: that would pull jobs south. An enterprise zone makes the northern town more attractive.
wrong.tax: Not quite: higher taxes would put the firm off. An enterprise zone lowers them.

idk.hint: Which option makes it cheaper for a business to set up in the north?

steps.answerWhy: An enterprise zone, with lower taxes, makes the northern town more attractive to the firm.

steps.prompt: In one line: name two strategies to reduce the north–south divide.
points: one strategy, such as devolution, enterprise zones or better transport
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: two strategies to reduce the north–south divide are devolution to city mayors and enterprise zones with lower taxes.

keyPoints.heading: The UK's place in the wider world

steps.text: The UK is linked to the rest of the world in many ways.
Trade: the UK buys and sells goods and services worldwide, and London is one of the world's biggest centres for banking and finance.
Culture: British music, films, television, football and the English language are known around the world.
Transport: airports such as Heathrow and ports such as Felixstowe connect the UK to every continent.
Electronic communication: undersea internet cables link the UK to Europe and North America.

The European Union, or EU, is a group of European countries that trade freely with each other. The UK left it, so trade with the EU now has more checks and paperwork, though the EU is still a major partner.

The Commonwealth is a group of countries, most of them once ruled by Britain, that work together on trade, development and shared values. The UK is a member: a political link, countries working together through a group.

steps.question: Which of these is a political link between the UK and other countries?
steps.right: Yes: the Commonwealth is a group of countries working together, a political and economic link.

wrong.other: Not quite: membership of the Commonwealth.
wrong.cable: Not quite: cables are an electronic communication link. The Commonwealth is a political link.
wrong.air: Not quite: Heathrow is a transport link. The Commonwealth is a political link.

idk.hint: Political links are about countries working together through groups. Which option is a group of countries?

steps.answerWhy: Membership of the Commonwealth is a political link.

steps.prompt: In one line: how has leaving the EU changed the UK's trade with the EU?
points: trade with the EU now has more checks and paperwork
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: since leaving the EU, UK trade with the EU has more checks and paperwork, though the EU is still a major partner.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: which of these is a traditional industry?

wrong.w1: Not quite: software design is new knowledge work. Coal mining is traditional.
wrong.w2: Not quite: banking is a service. Coal mining is traditional.

steps.answerWhy: Coal mining is one of the UK's traditional industries.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: what is a post-industrial economy?

options.text: One where most people work in services
One with no factories at all

steps.right: Yes: most people work in services.

wrong.other: Not quite: one where most people work in services.
wrong.w1: Not quite: some factories remain. Most people work in services.
wrong.w2: Not quite: farming is under 1% of the UK economy. Most people work in services.

steps.answerWhy: A post-industrial economy is one where most people work in services.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: what is the north–south divide?

options.text: The gap in wealth and health between the south-east and much of the rest of the UK
The border between England and Scotland
The difference between towns and the countryside

steps.right: Yes: on average the south-east is richer and people live longer.

wrong.other: Not quite: the gap in wealth and health between the south-east and much of the rest of the UK.
wrong.w1: Not quite: it is a gap in wealth and health, not a border.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it is a gap between the south-east and much of the rest of the UK, not between town and country.

steps.answerWhy: The north–south divide is the gap in wealth and health between the south-east and much of the UK.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: which is an example of more sustainable industry?

options.text: Toyota at Burnaston using solar and wind power

wrong.w1: Not quite: coal mining causes pollution. Toyota at Burnaston uses solar and wind power.
wrong.w2: Not quite: a road is infrastructure. Toyota at Burnaston is the sustainable industry example.

steps.answerWhy: Toyota at Burnaston uses renewable energy, a sustainable example.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: what is rural depopulation?

options.text: People leaving the countryside for towns and cities

steps.right: Yes: people, especially the young, leaving the countryside.

wrong.other: Not quite: people leaving the countryside for towns and cities.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is rural growth. Depopulation is people leaving.
wrong.w2: Not quite: depopulation is about people leaving the countryside.

steps.answerWhy: Rural depopulation is people leaving the countryside.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: which group is the UK still a member of?

wrong.w1: Not quite: the UK left the EU. It is still in the Commonwealth.
wrong.w2: Not quite: the UK is still in the Commonwealth.

steps.answerWhy: The UK left the EU but is still in the Commonwealth.
